gloss: woman, wife; man, mortal man; be desperately sick
summary: The spelling אנש holds three groups of words. אִשָּׁה is a woman, and a wife: the one built from the man and brought to him (Gen 2:22–24); its plural is נָשִׁים. אֱנוֹשׁ, with Aramaic אֱנָשׁ, is man and mankind, used most where man is set against God as one who dies (Psa 103:15; Isa 51:12), and כְּבַר אֱנָשׁ, “one like a son of man”, is the one who receives the kingdom in Dan 7:13. The verb אָנַשׁ is to be sick past healing (Jer 15:18). The cognates show two older sounds behind the ש: ṯ in “woman” (Arabic ʾunṯā, Ugaritic aṯt, Aramaic אנתתא) and š in “man, people” and in the plural “women” (Arabic ʾins, nās, nisāʾ; Aramaic אנשא, נשין), so that one Hebrew spelling covers what the other languages keep apart.

words.summary: A woman, and with a man’s name or a suffix his wife (construct אֵשֶׁת, אִשְׁתּוֹ); the plural in use is נָשִׁים, a separate word below, and the 781 uses counted here include its 212. Scripture’s own account of the word is Gen 2:23: “this one shall be called אִשָּׁה, for from אִישׁ this one was taken”. She is named beside the man as taken out of him, and the two words are paired from then on (אִישׁ וְאִשָּׁה). The doubled שׁ of אִשָּׁה answers to an n that the other languages keep (Arabic ʾunṯā, Sabaean ʾnṯt, Aramaic אנתתא): ʾinšā became ʾiššā, which is why the word is filed under אנש and not under איש, which has no doubling. Those languages have ṯ in this word, and š in their words for man and people; Hebrew writes both ש, so in Hebrew the woman’s name and the man’s sound together, as Gen 2:23 uses them. The š cognates of אֱנוֹשׁ and נָשִׁים are therefore counted against this word in the evidence table: that is the split in the spelling, not a doubt about the word’s meaning.

senses.definition: A female human being, set beside or against אִישׁ, a man: the one Yahweh God built from the man’s rib.

evidence.note: “Yahweh God built the rib which he had taken from the man לְאִשָּׁה, and brought her to the man.”
“This one shall be called אִשָּׁה, for from אִישׁ this one was taken”: the name is given beside the man’s and for her origin out of him.
אִישׁ אוֹ־אִשָּׁה, “a man or a woman”: the two together are everyone.
A man’s things shall not be on אִשָּׁה, nor shall a man wear שִׂמְלַת אִשָּׁה: the two are kept distinct.
הָאִשָּׁה saw that the tree was good for food, ate, and gave also to her husband.
“Every אִשָּׁה wise of heart spun with her hands.”
Deborah, אִשָּׁה נְבִיאָה, “a woman, a prophetess”, and in the same verse אֵשֶׁת לַפִּידוֹת, “wife of Lappidoth”.
אָדָם יְלוּד אִשָּׁה, “man, born of woman, few of days and full of trouble”.
“One אָדָם among a thousand I found, but אִשָּׁה among all these I did not find.”
Paul on Gen 2:22–23: “man is not from woman, but woman from man”, and she was created for the man.

senses.definition: A woman as belonging to a man by marriage: with a suffix, or in construct before his name. A betrothed woman is already called so.

evidence.note: “A man shall leave his father and his mother and cleave בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ, and they shall become one flesh.”
הָאִשָּׁה whom Abimelech took is בְּעֻלַת בָּעַל, “married to a husband”: the same woman is Abraham’s אִשָּׁה (Gen 20:2).
“You shall not covet אֵשֶׁת רֵעֶךָ”, your neighbour’s wife.
הָאָדָם וְאִשְׁתּוֹ, “the man and his wife”.
“You shall take אִשָּׁה for my son, for Isaac.”
Jacob of Rachel before the marriage: “Give me אִשְׁתִּי, for my days are fulfilled.”
The betrothed girl is אֵשֶׁת רֵעֵהוּ, “his neighbour’s wife”.
“Boaz took Ruth, and she became his לְאִשָּׁה.”
“He who finds אִשָּׁה finds good, and obtains favour from Yahweh.”
אֵשֶׁת נְעוּרֶיךָ … אֵשֶׁת בְּרִיתֶךָ, “the wife of your youth … the wife of your covenant”.
Jesus quotes Gen 2:24; the Peshitta has לַאנתְּתֵה, “to his wife”.

senses.definition: The people in covenant with Yahweh spoken of as his wife: faithful, treacherous, put away or taken back.

evidence.note: “Yahweh has called you like אִשָּׁה forsaken and grieved in spirit, and אֵשֶׁת נְעוּרִים when she is rejected”; verse 5: “your husband is your Maker”.
“She is not אִשְׁתִּי, and I am not her husband.”
“As אִשָּׁה deals treacherously with her companion, so you have dealt treacherously with me, house of Israel.”
Jerusalem: הָאִשָּׁה הַמְּנָאָפֶת, the adulterous wife who takes strangers instead of her husband.
“Go, love אִשָּׁה loved by a friend and an adulteress, like the love of Yahweh for the sons of Israel.”

senses.definition: The female of a pair of animals, beside אִישׁ for the male.

evidence.note: Of every clean beast seven and seven, אִישׁ וְאִשְׁתּוֹ, “a male and his female”; of the unclean two, אִישׁ וְאִשְׁתּוֹ.

senses.definition: With אֲחוֹתָהּ “her sister” or רְעוּתָהּ “her companion”: each one to the other, said of women and also of things and creatures spoken of in the feminine, as אִישׁ … אָחִיו is said of men.

evidence.note: Five curtains joined אִשָּׁה אֶל־אֲחֹתָהּ, “each to her sister”: curtains, not women.
The living creatures’ wings joined אִשָּׁה אֶל־אֲחוֹתָהּ.
The hawks gathered אִשָּׁה רְעוּתָהּ, “each with her mate”; so verse 16.
Of women: “teach your daughters wailing, וְאִשָּׁה רְעוּתָהּ a lament”.
Of the flock: “let them eat אִשָּׁה the flesh of רְעוּתָהּ”.

evidence.locator: Gen.2.22, לְאִשָּׁה → γυναῖκα; Gen.2.23, אִשָּׁה → γυνή; Gen.2.24, בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ → γυναῖκα; Gen.3.15 → γυναικός; Job.14.1 → γυναικός; γυνή renders אִשָּׁה ×688

evidence.note: Gen 2:24 quoted: “and shall be joined τῇ γυναικὶ αὐτοῦ, and the two shall be one flesh”.
Gen 2:24 quoted, and applied to Christ and the ecclesia (verse 32).
Gen 2:22–23 expounded: γυνὴ ἐξ ἀνδρός, “woman from man”.
“God sent his son, γενόμενον ἐκ γυναικός”, born of a woman: the Hebrew יְלוּד אִשָּׁה (Job 14:1).
ἐν γεννητοῖς γυναικῶν, “among those born of women”.

opposites.note: Man and woman, husband and wife: the pair from Gen 2:23 on. מֵאִישׁ וְעַד־אִשָּׁה, “from man to woman”, is everyone.

evidence.note: אִישָׁהּ, “her husband”.

phrases.gloss: a man’s wife, his neighbour’s wife: a married woman
one born of woman: a mortal man
each to the other (of feminine things)

words.summary: The plural that serves אִשָּׁה (construct נְשֵׁי, with suffixes נָשָׁיו, נְשֵׁיכֶם); אִשָּׁה’s own plural אִשֹּׁת occurs once (Ezk 23:44). The database files its tokens under אִשָּׁה’s key, so no uses are counted here: 212 of that word’s 781 are this plural. It is formed as אֲנָשִׁים “men” is, without the א, and the languages that keep ṯ and š apart show š here beside ṯ in the singular: Aramaic has אנתתא “woman” but נְשִׁין, נֵשֵׁא “women” (so Dan 6:25, and the Peshitta in Mat 5:28 beside Mat 27:55), and Arabic has ʾunṯā “female” but nisāʾ, niswa “women”. So the plural belongs by sound with אֱנוֹשׁ and אֲנָשִׁים, the “people” words, and the singular with the ṯ words; the ṯ cognates count against it in the evidence table for that reason.

senses.definition: Women, as a group beside the men (אֲנָשִׁים) and the little ones.

evidence.note: “Assemble the people, הָאֲנָשִׁים וְהַנָּשִׁים וְהַטַּף, the men and the women and the little ones.”
The assembly מֵאִישׁ וְעַד־אִשָּׁה, and in verse 3 הָאֲנָשִׁים וְהַנָּשִׁים: the plural pair answers the singular pair.
Joshua read before all the assembly, וְהַנָּשִׁים וְהַטַּף.
“Blessed מִנָּשִׁים, above women, is Jael.”
נְשֵׁי מִדְיָן, “the women of Midian”.
The sons gather wood, the fathers kindle the fire, וְהַנָּשִׁים knead dough.
“Blessed are you among women”: the Peshitta has בְּנֵשֵׁא, the same plural, as Jdg 5:24.

senses.gloss: women, as a figure of fighting men who have lost heart
senses.definition: Warriors whose strength has failed are said to be, or to become, women.

evidence.note: “The warriors of Babylon have ceased to fight … their might has dried up, הָיוּ לְנָשִׁים.”
“In that day Egypt will be כַּנָּשִׁים, and will tremble and fear.”
“Your people are נָשִׁים in your midst.”
The sword on the mixed company, “and they will become לְנָשִׁים”.

senses.definition: The wives of a man, or of a company of men.

evidence.note: “Lamech took for himself שְׁתֵּי נָשִׁים”: the first man with two wives.
Elkanah had שְׁתֵּי נָשִׁים, Hannah and Peninnah.
“They took for themselves נָשִׁים from all whom they chose.”
The king “shall not multiply נָשִׁים for himself, that his heart not turn aside”.
Solomon had seven hundred נָשִׁים, princesses, “and נָשָׁיו turned away his heart”.
“We have taken נָשִׁים נָכְרִיּוֹת, foreign wives, from the peoples of the land.”

opposites.note: Men and women: the two plurals are made alike and stand together.

phrases.gloss: the way of women: the monthly flow
the women and the little ones

words.summary: Man, and mankind as a whole: a word of the poetry (the Psalms, Job, Isaiah), never with the article and never in the plural. Its plural in form is אֲנָשִׁים, which serves אִישׁ (entry `ish`). Most of its uses set man against God as the one who is frail, sins and dies; whether that colour comes from the verb אָנַשׁ “be sick past healing” cannot be shown from the cognates, which keep “people” (Akkadian nišū) and “be weak” (Akkadian enēšu) apart, so it rests on scripture’s use alone. Of the 49 tokens counted, seven are the name Enosh (Gen 4:26; 5:6–11; 1Ch 1:1), which has the same spelling and its own entry. The ṯ cognates of אִשָּׁה count against the word in the evidence table: they are the other older sound in this spelling.

senses.definition: Human beings as a kind: collective, beside אָדָם and בֶּן־אָדָם.

evidence.note: מָה־אֱנוֹשׁ כִּי־תִזְכְּרֶנּוּ וּבֶן־אָדָם כִּי תִפְקְדֶנּוּ, “what is man that you remember him, and the son of man that you visit him?”
“I would make their memory cease מֵאֱנוֹשׁ, from among mankind.”
Wine gladdens לְבַב־אֱנוֹשׁ, and bread sustains לְבַב־אֱנוֹשׁ.
“אֱנוֹשׁ does not know its worth, and it is not found in the land of the living.”
“The dwellers of the earth are burned, and אֱנוֹשׁ is left few.”
“Every אָדָם has looked on it; אֱנוֹשׁ beholds from afar.”
Psa 8:5 quoted, and said to be fulfilled in Jesus (verse 9).

senses.gloss: man as frail and mortal, set against God
senses.definition: Man as he is before God: one whose days are like grass, who returns to dust, who cannot be righteous or strong against his Maker.

evidence.note: אֱנוֹשׁ כֶּחָצִיר יָמָיו, “man, his days are like grass”; verse 14, “he remembers that we are dust”.
“Who are you, that you fear מֵאֱנוֹשׁ יָמוּת, man who dies, and the son of man who is given up as grass?”
“You turn אֱנוֹשׁ back to dust, and say, Return, sons of man.”
“Arise, Yahweh, let not אֱנוֹשׁ prevail … let the nations know that they are אֱנוֹשׁ.”
הַאֱנוֹשׁ מֵאֱלוֹהַּ יִצְדָּק, “shall man be more righteous than God?”
“How shall אֱנוֹשׁ be righteous with God, and how shall one born of woman be clean?”
אֱנוֹשׁ רִמָּה, “man, a maggot, and the son of man, a worm”.
Job to God: “Do you see as אֱנוֹשׁ sees? Are your days as the days of אֱנוֹשׁ?”
“God is greater מֵאֱנוֹשׁ.”
“Is there not hard service לֶאֱנוֹשׁ on earth, and are not his days like the days of a hireling?”
Asa: “Yahweh, you are our God; let not אֱנוֹשׁ hold strength against you.”
“That אֱנוֹשׁ, who is of the earth, may terrify no more.”

senses.definition: A single man, where the context points to one: “the man who…”, “a man of my…”.

evidence.note: “But it was you, אֱנוֹשׁ כְּעֶרְכִּי, a man my equal, my companion and my familiar friend.”
כֹּל אֱנוֹשׁ שְׁלוֹמִי, “every man of my peace”, watching for my stumbling.
אַשְׁרֵי אֱנוֹשׁ יַעֲשֶׂה־זֹּאת, “happy the man who does this, and the son of man who holds to it”.
“Happy אֱנוֹשׁ whom God corrects.”
“Write on it בְּחֶרֶט אֱנוֹשׁ, with a man’s stylus”: in common writing.
“I will make אֱנוֹשׁ rarer than fine gold, and אָדָם than the gold of Ophir.”

evidence.locator: Psa.8.5, אֱנוֹשׁ → ἄνθρωπος; Psa.103.15 → ἄνθρωπος; Isa.51.12 → ἀνθρώπου; Job.25.6 → ἄνθρωπος; ἄνθρωπος renders אֱנוֹשׁ ×28

evidence.note: Psa 8:5 quoted: τί ἐστιν ἄνθρωπος ὅτι μιμνῄσκῃ αὐτοῦ, ἢ υἱὸς ἀνθρώπου ὅτι ἐπισκέπτῃ αὐτόν.

parallels.note: אֱנוֹשׁ in the first line and אָדָם or בֶּן־אָדָם in the second, or the reverse (Psa 144:3; Job 36:25): the two name the same creature.
אֱנוֹשׁ beside גֶּבֶר, a man in his strength, where both are measured against God.
Man and “one born of woman” in the two lines: the root’s two nouns side by side.

opposites.note: Man against God (אֱלוֹהַּ, אֵל): in righteousness, in sight, in length of days, in greatness.

phrases.gloss: son of man: a human being
the man of my peace: my friend

words.summary: The Aramaic of Daniel and Ezra for a man and for mankind (emphatic אֲנָשָׁא), the same word as Hebrew אֱנוֹשׁ with ā for ō. It occurs 25 times (Dan 2:10 to 7:13; Ezr 4:11; 6:11); the 134 tokens counted under its key include some 110 of Hebrew אֲנָשִׁים, filed here by spelling, which are the plural of אִישׁ. Dan 4:14 has that Hebrew plural, אֲנָשִׁים, in the Aramaic itself. The ṯ cognates of אִשָּׁה count against it in the evidence table: they are the other older sound in this spelling.

senses.definition: A human being, any person: with כָּל, “every man, whoever”; with a negative, “no one”; set against a god.

evidence.note: לָא־אִיתַי אֲנָשׁ עַל־יַבֶּשְׁתָּא, “there is not a man on the dry land who can show the king’s matter”.
Whoever asks a petition מִן־כָּל־אֱלָהּ וֶאֱנָשׁ, “of any god or man”, except of the king.
כָל־אֱנָשׁ who hears the sound of the horn shall fall down.
“Fingers of יַד־אֱנָשׁ, a man’s hand, came out and wrote.”
כָל־אֱנָשׁ who alters this word, a beam shall be pulled from his house.
“Your servants, אֱנָשׁ עֲבַר־נַהֲרָה, the men of Beyond the River”: collective, the people of a place.

senses.definition: אֲנָשָׁא, human beings as a kind: those among whom a man lives, over whose kingdom the Most High rules, and who are other than the beasts.

evidence.note: “That the living may know that the Most High rules בְּמַלְכוּת אֲנָשָׁא, in the kingdom of men, and gives it to whom he will, and sets up over it the lowest of men.”
“They will drive you מִן־אֲנָשָׁא, and your dwelling will be with the beast of the field”: men against beasts; fulfilled in verse 30.
“Let his heart be changed מִן־אֲנָשָׁא, and let a beast’s heart be given him.”
The first beast was made to stand on two feet כֶּאֱנָשׁ, “like a man”, and לְבַב אֱנָשׁ, “a man’s heart”, was given to it.
In the little horn, “eyes like עַיְנֵי אֲנָשָׁא, the eyes of a man”.
“They will mix themselves בִּזְרַע אֲנָשָׁא, with the seed of men, but they will not cleave one to another.”

senses.gloss: (בַּר אֱנָשׁ, בְּנֵי אֲנָשָׁא) a son of man, the sons of men
senses.definition: With בַּר “son”: one of mankind, a human being; in the plural, men. In Dan 7:13 the one who comes with the clouds of the heavens is כְּבַר אֱנָשׁ, “like a son of man”, after four kingdoms seen as beasts.

evidence.note: “Behold, with the clouds of the heavens כְּבַר אֱנָשׁ was coming, and he reached the Ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.”
What is given him: “dominion and glory and a kingdom, that all peoples, nations and languages should serve him”.
“Wherever בְּנֵי־אֲנָשָׁא dwell, the beast of the field and the bird of the heavens he has given into your hand.”
“He was driven מִן־בְּנֵי אֲנָשָׁא, from the sons of men, and his heart was made like the beasts’.”
Jesus applies Dan 7:13 to himself: “you will see the Son of man sitting at the right hand of power and coming on the clouds of heaven”; Peshitta בְּרֵהּ דְּאנָשָׁא.
“They will see the Son of man coming on the clouds of heaven with power and great glory.”
“In the midst of the lampstands one like a son of man”: Dan 7:13’s wording.

greek.gloss: man, human being; (υἱὸς ἀνθρώπου) son of man

evidence.locator: Dan.7.13, כְּבַר אֱנָשׁ → ὡς υἱὸς ἀνθρώπου; Dan.2.38, בְּנֵי־אֲנָשָׁא → ἀνθρώπων; ἄνθρωπος renders אֱנָשׁ ×7

evidence.note: τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου … ἐρχόμενον ἐπὶ τῶν νεφελῶν τοῦ οὐρανοῦ: Dan 7:13 with Psa 110:1.
The Son of man coming on the clouds of heaven.
ὅμοιον υἱῷ ἀνθρώπου, “like a son of man”.
On the white cloud, one sitting “like a son of man”.

opposites.note: Man and beast: Nebuchadnezzar is driven from men to live with the beast of the field, and the kingdoms are beasts until one like a son of man comes.
God or man: the two of whom a petition might be asked.

phrases.gloss: one like a son of man

words.summary: Nine uses: the passive participle אָנוּשׁ, אֲנוּשָׁה, of a wound, a pain, a day or the heart, and once the niphal of a child struck with sickness. Its own verses fix the sense (a wound that “refuses to be healed”, Jer 15:18). Its tie to the root’s nouns is not shown: the one cognate verb, Akkadian enēšu “be weak”, is a different word in Akkadian from nišū “people” and aššatu “wife”, and Akkadian cannot say whether its š was š or ṯ. Arabic ʾanīṯ “soft”, of the ṯ root of “female”, is recorded as possible only. That אֱנוֹשׁ is so often man as frail and dying sits well with the verb, but no verse joins the two.

senses.gloss: incurable, of a wound or pain
senses.definition: Of a blow, a breaking or a pain: so grave that it does not heal.

evidence.note: “Why is my pain perpetual, וּמַכָּתִי אֲנוּשָׁה מֵאֲנָה הֵרָפֵא, and my wound incurable, refusing to be healed?”: the verse explains the word.
אָנוּשׁ לְשִׁבְרֵךְ נַחְלָה מַכָּתֵךְ, “your breaking is incurable, your wound is grievous”; yet verse 17, “I will heal you of your wounds”.
“Why do you cry over your breaking? אָנוּשׁ מַכְאֹבֵךְ, because of the greatness of your iniquity.”
כִּי אֲנוּשָׁה מַכּוֹתֶיהָ, “her wounds are incurable, for it has come to Judah”.
The harvest a heap “in the day of sickness and כְאֵב אָנוּשׁ, incurable pain”.
אָנוּשׁ חִצִּי בְלִי־פָשַׁע, “my arrow (wound) is incurable, without transgression”.

senses.gloss: desperately sick, of the heart; disastrous, of a day
senses.definition: Carried over from the body: the heart as sick beyond cure, and a day of calamity as a day of mortal sickness.

evidence.note: עָקֹב הַלֵּב מִכֹּל וְאָנֻשׁ הוּא, “the heart is deceitful above all, and it is incurably sick; who can know it?”
וְיוֹם אָנוּשׁ לֹא הִתְאַוֵּיתִי, “the day of sickness I have not desired”: the day of disaster Jeremiah foretold.
The answer in the same chapter: “Heal me, Yahweh, and I shall be healed.”

senses.definition: To be struck with a sickness that ends in death.

evidence.note: “Yahweh struck the child that Uriah’s wife bore to David, וַיֵּאָנַשׁ”; on the seventh day the child died (verse 18).

parallels.note: אָנוּשׁ beside נַחְלָה “sick, grievous” (niphal participle of חָלָה).

opposites.note: What is אָנוּשׁ refuses healing; only Yahweh heals it.

phrases.gloss: the day of mortal sickness, of disaster

words.summary: The Aramaic plural “women, wives”, once in scripture’s Aramaic, with a suffix. It has š, as Hebrew נָשִׁים has, where the Aramaic singular (Peshitta אַנְתְּתָא) has t for older ṯ. The ṯ cognates of אִשָּׁה count against it in the evidence table: they are the other older sound in this spelling.

senses.definition: The wives of a company of men.

evidence.note: The accusers were thrown into the lions’ den, “they, בְּנֵיהוֹן וּנְשֵׁיהוֹן, their sons and their wives”.

words.gloss: man, mankind; (אנָשׁ) anyone, a certain one; (לָא אנָשׁ) no one; (בְּרֵהּ דְּאנָשָׁא) the Son of man
words.summary: The Peshitta’s אנשא (the א written, not sounded): mankind, people, and in the absolute אנָשׁ the ordinary word for “anyone, someone”, with לָא “no one”. “The Son of man” is always בְּרֵהּ דְּאנָשָׁא, “his son, of man”. The ṯ cognates of אִשָּׁה count against it in the evidence table: they are the other older sound in this spelling.

senses.definition: Human beings as a kind; people.

evidence.note: “Through one man (בַּרְנָשָׁא) sin entered the world … and so death passed on all בְּנַי אנָשָׁא, the sons of men.”
“Good hope לַבְנַי אנָשָׁא, to the sons of men.”
“Who do אנָשָׁא, people, say that I am?”

senses.gloss: anyone, a certain one; no one
senses.definition: The absolute אנָשׁ as an indefinite pronoun: anyone, each one, and with a negative no one.

evidence.note: לָא אנָשׁ מֶשְׁכַּח, “no one can serve two masters”.
“He had no need that אנָשׁ, anyone, should testify to him about any man.”
אנָשׁ אַנְתְּתֵה, “let each man have his wife”.

senses.definition: The title Jesus uses of himself, and Psa 8:5’s “son of man”.

evidence.note: “You will see לַבְרֵהּ דְּאנָשָׁא sitting at the right hand of power and coming on the clouds of heaven”: Dan 7:13.
“The Son of man is lord of the sabbath.”
Psa 8:5: “what is man (גַּבְרָא) that you remember him, וּבְרֵהּ דְּאנָשָׁא that you visit him?”
The angels of God ascending and descending to בְּרֵהּ דְּאנָשָׁא.

words.gloss: a human being, a man; (pl. בְּנַינָשָׁא) human beings, people
words.summary: בַּר “son” and נָשָׁא written as one word: the Peshitta’s ordinary word for a human being, where the Greek has ἄνθρωπος. It is Dan 7:13’s בַּר אֱנָשׁ in everyday use, and Ugaritic bnš “man” is made the same way. The ṯ cognates of אִשָּׁה count against it in the evidence table: they are the other older sound in this spelling.

senses.definition: One of mankind, man or woman, as distinct from God, from angels and from beasts.

evidence.note: “The sabbath was made for בַּרְנָשָׁא, and not בַּרְנָשָׁא for the sabbath.”
“Not by bread alone does בַּרְנָשָׁא live” (Deu 8:3, Hebrew הָאָדָם).
“How much more is בַּרְנָשָׁא than a sheep!”
Paul and Barnabas: “we also are בְּנַינָשָׁא, subject to suffering like you”.
“Elijah was בַּרְנָשָׁא subject to suffering like us.”
“As through בַּרְנָשָׁא came death, so also through בַּרְנָשָׁא comes the resurrection of the dead.”
“One like the form of בַּרְנָשָׁא”: Dan 7:13’s כְּבַר אֱנָשׁ; so Rev 14:14.
“It is appointed לַבְנַינָשָׁא to die once.”

words.summary: The Peshitta’s word for a woman and a wife, written אנתתא with the נ unsounded (ʾattəṯā). Its t is the Aramaic for older ṯ, the sound Arabic ʾunṯā and Ugaritic aṯt keep, where Hebrew אִשָּׁה has שׁ. Its plural is נֵשֵׁא, below, with š. The š cognates of אֱנוֹשׁ and נָשִׁים count against it in the evidence table: they are the other older sound in this spelling.

senses.definition: A female human being.

evidence.note: “Man is not from אַנְתְּתָא, but אַנְתְּתָא from man”: Gen 2:22–23.
“Everyone who looks at אַנְתְּתָא to desire her.”
“God sent his son, and he came to be מֶן אַנְתְּתָא, from a woman.”

senses.definition: A man’s wife.

evidence.note: Gen 2:24: “a man will leave his father and his mother and cleave לַאנתְּתֵה, to his wife”.
The same quotation.
“I will show you the bride, אַנְתְּתֵה דְּאֶמְרָא, the wife of the Lamb.”

words.summary: The plural that serves אַנְתְּתָא in the Peshitta, as נָשִׁים serves אִשָּׁה: the singular has t (older ṯ), the plural š. SEDRA files its forms under the singular’s lexeme. The ṯ cognates of אִשָּׁה count against it in the evidence table: they are the other older sound in this spelling.

senses.definition: Women.

evidence.note: “There were also many נֵשֵׁא there, looking on from afar.”
“Blessed are you בְּנֵשֵׁא, among women.”
“Among those born of נֵשֵׁא.”
The angel said לְנֵשֵׁא, to the women.

senses.definition: Wives.

evidence.note: “Husbands, love נֵשַׁיכּוֹן, your wives, as the Messiah loved his ecclesia.”

words.summary: כֻּל “all” and נָשׁ “man” written as one word. The ṯ cognates of אִשָּׁה count against it in the evidence table: they are the other older sound in this spelling.

senses.definition: Every person.

evidence.note: “That כֻּלְנָשׁ might believe through him.”
“That כֻּלְנָשׁ may honour the Son as he honours the Father.”
“Shall be the slave of כֻּלְנָשׁ.”

words.gloss: humanity, mankind; people, one’s own people
words.summary: The abstract of אנָשָׁא, three times in the Peshitta New Testament. The ṯ cognates of אִשָּׁה count against it in the evidence table: they are the other older sound in this spelling.

senses.definition: Mankind as a nature; a body of people; one’s kinsfolk.

evidence.note: Every nature of beasts and birds is subjected לַכְיָנָא דְּאנָשׁוּתָא, “to the nature of humanity”.
“They sought him among אנָשׁוּתְהוֹן, their people”, their kinsfolk.
“To stir up and trouble לְאנָשׁוּתָא, the people.”

cognates.gloss: female; a female, of mankind or of any creature
cognates.note: The word for a woman in the other languages, in Arabic the general word for “female”, set against ذَكَر “male” as אִשָּׁה is against אִישׁ and against זָכָר. It keeps the n that Hebrew has taken into the doubled שׁ, and its ṯ is the older sound behind that ש. The root’s other words are “be feminine”, and of land and iron “soft”.

evidence.note: “Female; feminine; of the female, or feminine, sex, or gender; contr. of ذَكَرٌ: an epithet applied to anything of that sex or gender … اِمْرَأَةٌ أُنْثَى [A feminine woman,] means a perfect woman.”

cognates.note: Ugaritic writes ṯ and š with different letters and has ṯ here; the n is assimilated as in Hebrew (/ʾaṯṯat-/ from *-nṯ-).

evidence.note: “(< *-nṯ-) ‘woman’ (Akkad. aššatu, H. ʾiššā, Aram. ʾnth, Syr. ʾa(n)ttā, Arab. ʾunṯā(y))”; aṯt ṣdqh, KTU 1.14:I:12, “his legitimate wife”.
“woman, wife”.

cognates.note: Sabaean keeps both the n and the ṯ, and writes the singular also ʾṯt with the n assimilated.

evidence.note: “FEMALE; WOMAN; WIFE”; Ry 375/6–7 “a child, male or female”; R 4188/5 “the safety of their wives and children”.

cognates.note: The Targums’ word, the same as the Peshitta’s אַנְתְּתָא. Aramaic turns older ṯ into t and keeps š as š, so its t here beside the š of אֱנָשׁ and נְשִׁין shows the two sounds in one language.

evidence.note: “(אִתְּתָא) woman, wife. Targ. Job XXV, 4; a. fr.”: the Targum’s word for אִשָּׁה in יְלוּד אִשָּׁה.

cognates.note: “Wife” only; a woman in general is sinništu. The n is assimilated as in Hebrew. Akkadian š stands for older š and ṯ alike, so it does not show which is behind the ש. aššūtu, “marriage, the status of a wife”, is its abstract.

evidence.note: “wife”; 1,544 instances, Old Assyrian and Old Babylonian onward.
“marriage; status of a wife”.

cognates.note: Phoenician has the same senses as the Hebrew, including “female” of a sacrificial victim beside ʾš “male”, as Gen 7:2. Like Hebrew it writes one letter for š and ṯ.

evidence.note: “1. WOMAN” (KAI 26 A II 3/6, “in my days a woman walks alone”); “2. WIFE” (KAI 35.1/3, “my wife Amotastarte”); “5. FEMALE” (CIS i 5511.6, “every person, whether male or female”).

cognates.gloss: mankind; a human being; men, people
cognates.note: Arabic s answers to older š. ʾins is mankind as against the jinn, ʾinsān a human being of either sex, and بَنُو الإِنْسَانِ “the sons of man” is the sons of Adam, as בֶּן־אֱנוֹשׁ. The root’s verb ʾanisa is “be sociable, familiar”, and ʾinsī is “domestic, tame” as against waḥšī “wild”: compare Daniel’s man driven from men to live with the beasts (Dan 4:29).

evidence.note: “Mankind; the opposite of جِنٌّ; as also أَنَسٌ, and إِنْسَانٌ; the last being a gen. n., but applied to the male and female, and sing. and pl. … the pl. is … أُنَاسٌ, with which نَاسٌ is syn., being a contraction thereof … بَنُو الإِنْسَانِ means The sons of Adam.”
“Of, or belonging to, mankind; human … A human being; a man … [Domestic, as opposed to wild.]”

cognates.note: The Arabic plural “people”, said by the Arab grammarians to be ʾunās with its first syllable dropped: the same shortening as Hebrew נָשִׁים beside אֲנָשִׁים, Aramaic נָשָׁא beside אֲנָשָׁא, and Ugaritic nšm.

evidence.note: “is applied to Men, and to jinn … it is a pl. of إِنْسٌ, originally أُنَاسٌ”; Lane notes that others derive it from نَاسَ “move to and fro”.

cognates.note: The Arabic plural “women”, which has no singular of its own (a woman is imraʾa), as נָשִׁים has none. Its s is older š, not the ṯ of ʾunṯā “female”: Arabic too has the two sounds side by side. Lane’s lexicon has no article for the word in the vendored copy (its last parts are a supplement), so it is cited from the phrases where he glosses it.

evidence.note: “You say تِسْعَةُ رِجَالٍ [Nine men], and تِسْعُ نِسْوَةٍ [Nine women].”
Kur iv. 1, رِجَالًا كَثِيرًا وَنِسَآءً, “many men, and women”.

cognates.note: Ugaritic has š in “men” and ṯ in aṯt “woman”, written with different letters.

evidence.note: “‘men’ (cf. H. pl. ʾănāšīm, cf. Aram. coll. nāšā, Arab. coll. nās; cf. Akkad. pl. nišū)”.

cognates.note: “Son of man” written as one word, as the Peshitta’s בַּרְנָשָׁא; compare בֶּן־אֱנוֹשׁ (Psa 144:3) and בַּר אֱנָשׁ (Dan 7:13).

evidence.note: “bu-nu-šu … ‘man’ (< /bun-/ ‘son’ + /nōš-/ < *nāš ‘mankind’) (cf. ben-ʾĕnōš Ps 144:3; Aram. bar ʾĕnāš)”; bnš bnšm, KTU 3.5:16, “every man”.

cognates.note: Sabaean s¹ answers to older š; the same inscriptions have ʾnṯt “woman” with ṯ.

evidence.note: “MAN (cf ʾYS I); pejoratively, FELLOW”; R 3910/3 “(those who) buy any man or camel”.

cognates.gloss: human being, man; people; son of man, a human being
cognates.note: The Targums and Talmud continue Daniel’s word, with בַּר נָשׁ, “son of man”, as the everyday word for a person. Aramaic keeps š as š and turns ṯ into t, so the š here is the older š.

evidence.note: “being, esp. human being Dan. II, 10 … Ib. VII, 13 בר א׳ son of man (in Talm. freq. בר נש). Targ. O. Lev. XIII, 2 … Pl. אֵינָשִׁין … In Talm. mostly אִינְשֵׁי people.”
“= אִינָשׁ, only in בַּר נ׳ son of man, human being. Targ. Job VII, 1 … Pl. נָשָׁא, בְּנֵי נָשׁ.”

cognates.note: The Targums’ plural for נָשִׁים, with š, beside the singular אִנְתְּתָא with t: the Aramaic that keeps the two older sounds apart has one in the singular and the other in the plural.

evidence.note: “woman. Targ. Y. Deut. XXII, 5 … Pl. נְשִׁין, נְשַׁיָּא, נְשֵׁי. Targ. Ruth I, 4. Targ. Gen. VI, 2.”

cognates.gloss: people, mankind; the people of a king or a household
cognates.note: A plural, “people”, without the first syllable, as נָשִׁים, Arabic nās and Ugaritic nšm. Akkadian š does not show the older sound.

evidence.note: “humanity; people; troops”; 11,777 instances in every period.

cognates.note: An abstract in t- of the same base, “humankind”, as the Peshitta’s אנָשׁוּתָא.

evidence.note: “humankind; mankind; people”; 311 instances.

cognates.gloss: be or become weak; (of buildings) fall into ruin; (D) weaken
cognates.note: The one verb that answers to אָנַשׁ, with its adjective enšu “weak”. In Akkadian it is a different word from nišū “people”. The Hebrew is narrower: sick, and past healing.

evidence.note: “be(come) weak; dilapidate; make weak, weaken”; 271 instances.
“weak; weak (person)”.

cognates.gloss: soft: of land, plain and fruitful; of iron or a sword, soft, not sharp
cognates.note: Of the same Arabic root as ʾunṯā “female”; one Arab authority held softness to be the root’s first meaning and “female” to come from it, others the reverse. If אָנוּשׁ belongs here, the verb goes with אִשָּׁה (ṯ) and not with אֱנוֹשׁ (š); but “soft” is not “sick past healing”, and no Hebrew verse uses the verb of softness. No `sounds` is recorded for it, so that a merely possible cognate does not class the verb with the ṯ words.

evidence.note: “أَرْضٌ أَنِيثَةٌ Plain, even, or soft, land … حَدِيدٌ أَنِيثٌ Female iron … soft iron. And سَيْفٌ أَنِيثٌ … a sword that is not sharp.” Under the verb (p. 112): “said of iron, It was, or became, soft … Accord. to IAar, softness is the primary signification.”

doctrine.statement: Yahweh God caused a deep sleep to fall on the man, took one of his ribs, “built” it into a woman and brought her to the man, who said, “this one shall be called אִשָּׁה, for from אִישׁ this one was taken” (Gen 2:22–23). Jesus cites the account as what happened “from the beginning”: “he who made them from the beginning made them male and female” (Mat 19:4), and “from the beginning it was not so” (Mat 19:8). Paul reasons from its order: “man is not from woman, but woman from man”, and the woman was created for the man (1Co 11:8–9); “Adam was formed first, then Eve” (1Ti 2:13). From the verses: the first woman did not descend from earlier creatures; she was made by God from the first man on the day he was made, and both Jesus and Paul build on that as history.

From the making of the woman scripture draws its rule of marriage: “therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and cleave to אִשְׁתּוֹ, his wife, and they shall become one flesh” (Gen 2:24). Jesus quotes it and concludes, “they are not two, but one flesh; what God has joined, let man not separate” (Mat 19:5–6). Malachi calls her “the wife of your youth … your companion and the wife of your covenant”, to whom Yahweh is witness, and warns against dealing treacherously with her (Mal 2:14–15). “He who finds a wife finds good, and obtains favour from Yahweh” (Pro 18:22). From the verses: marriage is one man and one woman joined by God into one, a covenant he witnesses; Lamech’s two wives (Gen 4:19) and the wives who turned Solomon’s heart (1Ki 11:3) are recorded, not commended.

Yahweh speaks of Israel as his wife: “your husband is your Maker”, who calls her back “like a wife forsaken … a wife of youth when she is rejected” (Isa 54:5–6); when she is unfaithful, “she is not my wife, and I am not her husband” (Hos 2:4), yet “I will betroth you to me for ever” (Hos 2:21). Paul quotes Gen 2:24 and says, “this mystery is great, but I speak of Christ and of the ecclesia”, whom Christ loved and gave himself for (Eph 5:25, 31–32); he had betrothed the Corinthians “to one husband, to present a pure virgin to Christ” (2Co 11:2). At the end, “the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his wife has made herself ready” (Rev 19:7), and John is shown “the bride, the wife of the Lamb” (Rev 21:9). From the verses: the woman taken from the man’s side and joined to him is the pattern of the ecclesia, betrothed now and to be made one with Christ at his coming.

God said to the serpent, “I will put enmity between you and the woman (הָאִשָּׁה), and between your seed and her seed; he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel” (Gen 3:15). To be “born of woman” is to be a man, short of days and unclean: “man, born of woman, few of days and full of trouble” (Job 14:1); “how shall one born of woman be clean?” (Job 25:4). Paul says, “when the fulness of the time came, God sent his son, born of a woman, born under law” (Gal 4:4), and Hebrews, “since the children share in flesh and blood, he also in the same way shared in the same, that through death he might bring to nothing the one having the power of death” (Heb 2:14). From the verses: the promised deliverer is the woman’s seed, so a man of our own nature, and God’s son; it was by dying in that nature that he overcame.

Where scripture calls man אֱנוֹשׁ it most often says what he is beside God. “Man, his days are like grass; like a flower of the field so he flourishes; for the wind passes over it and it is gone”, for God “remembers that we are dust” (Psa 103:14–16). “You turn man back to dust” (Psa 90:3), as was said to Adam, “dust you are, and to dust you shall return” (Gen 3:19). He is “man who dies” (Isa 51:12), “a maggot” (Job 25:6), and the nations are to learn “that they are but men” (Psa 9:21). In the son of man “there is no salvation: his breath goes out, he returns to his ground; in that day his thoughts perish” (Psa 146:3–4), and “the dead know nothing” (Ecc 9:5). Paul says “this mortal must put on immortality” (1Co 15:53). From the verses: man is mortal through and through; nothing in him lives on in death, and immortality is something to be put on at the resurrection.

Jeremiah uses the word for a wound that will not heal of the heart: “the heart is deceitful above all things, and it is incurably sick (אָנֻשׁ); who can know it?” (Jer 17:9). Jesus says the same of its fruit: “from within, out of the heart of men, come evil thoughts, adulteries, fornications, murders … all these evil things come from within and defile the man” (Mrk 7:21–23); and James, “each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own desire; then desire, having conceived, bears sin, and sin, when it is full grown, brings forth death” (Jas 1:14–15). Jeremiah’s answer is a prayer, “heal me, Yahweh, and I shall be healed” (Jer 17:14), and to the people whose breaking was incurable Yahweh says, “I will heal you of your wounds” (Jer 30:12, 17). From the verses: the source of sin is man’s own heart, a sickness he cannot cure himself; the healing is God’s.

Daniel’s Aramaic sets man (אֱנָשׁ) against beast. Nebuchadnezzar is driven “from men” to dwell with the beasts, a beast’s heart given him in place of a man’s, “until you know that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men and gives it to whom he will” (Dan 4:13, 29). The four kingdoms that follow are four beasts “arising from the earth” (Dan 7:3, 17); then “one like a son of man” (כְּבַר אֱנָשׁ) comes with the clouds of the heavens to the Ancient of days and is given “dominion and glory and a kingdom, that all peoples, nations and languages should serve him”, a kingdom that will not be destroyed (Dan 7:13–14); and “the kingdom and the dominion and the greatness of the kingdoms under the whole heaven will be given to the people of the saints of the Most High” (Dan 7:27). Jesus takes the words to himself before the high priest: “you will see the Son of man sitting at the right hand of power and coming on the clouds of heaven” (Mat 26:64; so 24:30), and John sees “one like a son of man” (Rev 1:13; 14:14). Hebrews reads Psa 8, “what is man (אֱנוֹשׁ) … and the son of man”, of Jesus, made a little lower than the angels and crowned with glory, to whom all things are not yet seen subjected (Heb 2:6–9). From the verses: the one to whom God gives the kingdom is a man, of mankind and not a beast-power; he receives it from God, he comes to reign “under the whole heaven”, on the earth, and his people share it with him.

note: Drafted 2026-11-15. Root key אנש, as the brief and the database key it (entry_root gives אנש for a.eq.ab אִשָּׁה, a.ep.ab אֱנוֹשׁ, a.eo.aa אָנַשׁ, xa.az.ab אֱנָשׁ; no other entry has it). The entry is a `one spelling, one entry` case with a split behind ש: ṯ for אִשָּׁה (Arabic ʾunṯā, Ugaritic aṯt, Sabaean ʾnṯt, Aramaic אנתתא) and š for אֱנוֹשׁ / אֱנָשׁ and for the plural נָשִׁים / נְשִׁין (Arabic ʾins, nās, nisāʾ; Ugaritic nšm, bnš; Sabaean ʾns¹; Aramaic אנשא, נשין). The strongest evidence is inside scripture’s own Aramaic: the Peshitta’s singular אנתתא has t and its plural נֵשֵׁא has š (Dan 6:25 נְשֵׁיהוֹן too). Negative balances on אִשָּׁה, נָשִׁים, אֱנוֹשׁ and אֱנָשׁ in `lexicon-support` are this split and are explained in the words’ summaries. Gen 2:23 (אִשָּׁה … מֵאִישׁ) is treated as scripture’s own account of the name: the summary says the two words sound together in Hebrew and that the doubled שׁ answers to the n-forms; it does not call the naming a false etymology, and says nothing of which language is older. The reviewer should check that wording. Words: נָשִׁים is made a word of its own (n.fu.ae, a cross-reference key with 0 tokens) because its cognates and sound differ from the singular’s; its 212 tokens (surfaces with נש under a.eq.ab) are counted under אִשָּׁה. Aramaic נְשִׁין takes xa.ba.ab (Dan 6:25, root נשינ in entry_root); the brief listed the cross-reference xn.aq.ab instead, which has no tokens. Not included: אִישׁ and its plural אֲנָשִׁים (a.da.ab), drafted as entry `ish`; אֲנָשִׁים is in form the plural of אֱנוֹשׁ and the brief counts about 110 of its tokens under xa.az.ab by spelling. Zero-token cross-reference keys a.gd.ad, a.gl.ac (אֵשֶׁת), xn.aq.ab, a.eq.aa, a.ep.aa, xa.az.aa, xa.ba.aa are left unclaimed. a.ep.ab (49) and a.ep.ac (40, the name Enosh, names/enosh.json) overlap by spelling: only Gen 4:26; 5:6, 7, 9, 10, 11; 1Ch 1:1 are the name. The morphology gives אָנוּשׁ / אֲנוּשָׁה the root נוש; the tokens reach this entry through a.eo.aa. Syriac words are from SEDRA root 145 ܐܢܫ (lexemes 195 ܐܢܫܐ, 196 ܐܢܫܘܬܐ, 3462 ܟܠܢܫ, 3463 ܒܪܢܫܐ) and root 148, lexeme 199 ܐܢܬܬܐ, whose word forms include the plural ܢܫܐ; the plural is entered as its own word, with no `root` of its own, because the key נשא is the Hebrew root “lift” (entry nasa-lift). Greek: no loan. The Septuagint renders the verb once by ἠρρώστησεν (2Sa 12:15), a verb the New Testament does not use, so no Greek is recorded for it. Cognate leads not followed, for want of a page I could check: Geʿez ʾanəst “women” (Dillmann, Leslau; Biella p. 23 mentions it), Syriac ܢܫ “become weak” (which, if it has š, would put the verb with אֱנוֹשׁ), Old and Imperial Aramaic ʾnš / ʾnth (CAL, DNWSI), Akkadian in CAD (aššatu, nišū, enēšu, tenēšētu; the Oracc glossaries are cited), DULAT for Ugaritic inš / anš, Sabaean in SabaWeb. Akkadian enēšu begins with e-, which in Akkadian usually marks a lost guttural other than ʾ; if so it is not the root of nišū at all, and the verb’s place in this entry rests on spelling only. Segert’s and Biella’s pages were checked against the scans’ own page text (pdftotext), Krahmalkov’s from the running heads. Open questions for review: (1) whether אָנַשׁ should stay here or be a homograph; (2) the kin links from נָשִׁים to אִשָּׁה’s senses, which join words the sounds separate; (3) the doctrine statements, especially son-of-man (ben.json has a statement under the same topic) and bride-of-christ; (4) the Hebrew-script lemmas for the Syriac (אנָשָׁא written with unpointed א for the silent alaph).
